clinicalPearls: Sudden painful involuntary contractions, usually of the calf or small foot muscles, occurring during the sleep period
The cramp produces a palpably hard, tight muscle and is relieved by forceful stretching or massage of the affected muscle
Unlike restless legs syndrome, the problem is frank painful muscle contraction rather than an urge to move with relief on movement
Prevalence rises with age and cramps are common in pregnancy
Secondary contributors include dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, peripheral vascular or neurological disease and certain drugs
Management emphasises stretching, addressing reversible contributors and reviewing culprit medications
reference.pathophysiology: Sleep-related leg cramps arise from sustained involuntary hyperexcitable motor-unit discharge in a muscle, producing a sudden painful contraction; the tendency is increased by muscle shortening during sleep and by factors that alter neuromuscular excitability. Ageing, pregnancy, fluid and electrolyte shifts, and peripheral nerve or vascular disease can lower the threshold for these discharges. In many people the cramps are idiopathic, reflecting benign motor-neuron hyperexcitability rather than a defined underlying disease.
additionalDifferentials: Electrolyte disturbance (for example low potassium, calcium or magnesium)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis from the description and relief by stretching
Review for dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and culprit medications
Assessment for peripheral vascular and neurological disease when frequent
Targeted blood tests where a secondary cause is suspected
Further neurological evaluation if cramps are severe, generalised or progressive
redFlags: Cramps with progressive weakness, wasting or sensory loss
Features of significant peripheral arterial disease
Widespread or daytime cramps suggesting a systemic or neuromuscular disorder
reference.prognosis: The cramps are benign though disruptive to sleep; many respond to stretching and correction of reversible contributors, and idiopathic cases often fluctuate over time.
pitfalls: Confusing leg cramps with restless legs syndrome and mismanaging them
Overlooking peripheral vascular or neurological disease when cramps are frequent
Not reviewing medications that can provoke cramps
Missing correctable dehydration or electrolyte disturbance
references: American Academy of Sleep Medicine ICSD-3
Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine
management: Relieve the acute cramp by forceful passive stretching and massage of the affected calf or foot muscle
Recommend regular stretching of the calf and foot muscles before sleep as the first-line preventive measure
Identify and correct reversible contributors such as dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and peripheral vascular or neurological disease
Consider magnesium for pregnancy-associated cramps and reserve quinine only for severe refractory cases given its toxicity, with careful risk counselling
Reassure about the benign nature and arrange further neurological evaluation if cramps are severe, generalised or progressive
